Distal Biceps Tendon Rupture
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

Overview
Distal biceps tendon rupture may reduce supination strength and, to a lesser extent,
flexion strength and endurance. Rupture usually is diagnosed based on patient history
and physical examination findings. Radiographs are not necessary for diagnosis but may
demonstrate a small avulsion of the biceps tuberosity and aid in excluding other
pathology. Imaging studies such as MRI or ultrasonography may help plan surgical
management in patients undergoing delayed treatment. Myriad surgical techniques are
available. Evidence shows that surgical management results in slightly better supination
strength than nonsurgical management. Many patients elect to not have the tendon
reattached because they find decreased supination strength acceptable and can
accommodate for this decrease.
Epidemiology and Risk Factors
Distal biceps tendon ruptures most often occur in the dominant extremity of middle-aged
men.
A paucity of evidence is available on metabolic factors associated with distal biceps tendon
ruptures. Some suggested associations include anabolic steroids, smoking, and obesity.


Epidemiology and Risk Factors
The reported incidence of distal biceps tendon ruptures increased in the past decade.1
In 2010, the incidence of distal biceps ruptures was reported to be 1.2 per 100,000
patient-years. Recent studies suggest an incidence of 2.5 per 100,000 patient-years.2,3
Whether this represents more frequent diagnosis of rupture or an increased rate of
rupture remains unclear. Ruptures tend to occur in the dominant elbow of men (95%).
The mean patient age of men with a distal biceps rupture is 47 years.2-4 The mean age of
women with a distal biceps rupture is older than 60 years.3
Safran and Graham1 examined the demographics of affected individuals within a single
healthcare system to determine risk factors for distal biceps tendon rupture. They
reported that current cigarette smoking was associated with a 7.5-fold increased risk of
distal biceps tendon rupture. The PearlDiver Technologies national database was used to
estimate the national incidence of distal biceps tendon ruptures. A retrospective chart
review identified obesity as an independent risk factor for distal biceps tendon rupture.4
Kanayama et al5 studied bodybuilders and identified that those who used anabolic-
androgenic steroids were at increased risk for tendon rupture, particularly in the upper
extremity, including the distal biceps tendon.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The short and long heads of the biceps have distinct insertions on the radial tuberosity, and
the two heads coalesce to allow the biceps to function as a forearm supinator and, to a lesser
degree, an elbow flexor.
The height and protuberance of the radial tuberosity serves as a cam to maximize supination
torque.
The lacertus fibrosus originates from the distal aspect of the short head of the biceps tendon
and blends with the fascia of the ulnar aspect of the proximal forearm.

Anatomy and Biomechanics

The radial/bicipital tuberosity has a mean length of 22 to 26 mm and a mean width of
10.4 to 13.6 mm. The radial tuberosity is positioned 180° opposite the radial styloid. The
tuberosity has a protuberance just anterior to the footprint of the distal biceps tendon
insertion, which serves as a cam maximizing supination torque, especially in terminal
supination.3 In a biomechanical study, Schmidt et al6 identified that placing the tendon
in a trough measuring 7 mm wide by 10 mm long in the radial tuberosity resulted in a
biceps supination moment arm of 4.9 mm compared with 6.2 mm in intact control
subjects. This represents a 27% decrease in biceps supination moment arm with the
forearm in 60° of supination.6 In the same study, the biceps supination moment arm in
the supinated position correlated with tuberosity height.6 The mean length of the distal
biceps tendon insertion on the apex of the radial tuberosity is 15 to 21 mm, with a mean
width of 3.5 to 7 mm, which indicates that the tendon insertion occupies a portion of the
radial tuberosity rather than the entirety of the radial tuberosity.2
The biceps muscle is composed of two components: the short head of the biceps and
the long head of the biceps. As the confluence of the short head of the biceps tendon
and the long head of the biceps tendon approaches the insertion point, the tendon
rotates 90° externally, resulting in the more distal insertion of the short head of the
biceps tendon (Figure 1). This distal insertion of the short head gives it greater torque in
elbow flexion. The proximal insertion of the long head of the biceps provides a greater
lever arm for supination. Jarrett et al7 identified that the ratio of the flexion load to the
biceps load was 15% higher for the short head of the biceps tendon than for the long
head of the biceps tendon, demonstrating that the short head of the biceps tendon
played a more important role in elbow flexion. In that same cadaver model study, the
more distal insertion of the short head allowed it to be the more efficient supinator in
pronation, with an 8% higher moment arm, and in neutral, with a 13% higher moment
arm. With the forearm supinated 60°, the long head becomes the more efficient
supinator as the short head of the biceps tendon is nearly fully unwrapped, whereas the
more posterior and proximal position of the long head of the biceps tendon allows it to
still be partially wrapped, allowing for progression to terminal supination.7 Although
anatomic studies afford a good understanding of the anatomy of the distal biceps
tendon and its insertion points, available repair techniques do not fully reapproximate
normal anatomy; however, some represent a closer representation than others.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The mechanism of injury of distal biceps tendon ruptures usually involves an eccentric load
applied to the biceps.
The patient often reports feeling or hearing a pop and pain at the antecubital fossa.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Distal biceps tendon ruptures almost always occur at the site of insertion on the radial
tuberosity. Reports of distal biceps tendon ruptures at the mid-tendon and
musculotendinous junction are rare; similarly, bipolar ruptures are exceedingly rare. The
typical mechanism of injury for distal biceps tendon rupture involves an eccentric load
applied to an elbow that is actively flexed. The proposed mechanism of the rare
musculotendinous rupture in a series of six patients was eccentric contracture during
shoulder elevation, elbow extension, and forearm supination.8
Ruptures occur in patients with tendinopathy; however, pre-rupture symptoms are
uncommon. Conversely, patients with symptomatic tendinopathy are unlikely to
experience ruptures.
The distal biceps tendon is relatively hypovascular, which may contribute to
tendinopathy. Conversely, three major zones of blood supply exist from the radial
recurrent artery, posterior interosseous artery, and anterior interosseous artery. Zone 1
is a watershed zone, which typically is location in which ruptures occur, leaving behind a
small remnant of tendon on the tuberosity. Zone 2 is avascular, and zone 3 is
vascularized.
The distance between the lateral border of the ulna and the radial tuberosity decreases
by 48% from supination to pronation, which may result in mechanical impingement;

A partial tear of the biceps tendon may be misleading because this term variably is used
to refer to distal biceps tendinopathy or a functionally complete tear but anatomically
apparently incomplete tear. Acute rupture has been proposed to be isolated to the short
head, which inserts more distally along the tuberosity.9 Additional data are necessary to
determine how frequently this occurs and the degree to which it is associated with
ongoing symptoms that, in the past, were diagnosed as distal biceps tendinopathy.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
A patient history and a physical examination generally are sufficient to diagnose a distal biceps
tendon rupture.
Patients often report a pop during an activity involving an eccentric load to a flexed elbow.
This pop usually is followed by pain and ecchymosis of the elbow and proximal forearm.
If the lacertus fibrosis ruptures, the biceps will retract proximally into the brachium.
The resulting deformity is subtle, mostly related to loss of the prominence of the tendon in the
antecubital fossa, and not nearly as prominent as with rupture of the long head of the biceps
tendon in the shoulder, which gives rise to a more prominent Popeye muscle appearance.
The distal biceps tendon may no longer be palpable in the antecubital fossa, as evaluated by
the so-called hook test.
The retracted tendon often curls into a ball and can be felt just distal to the retracted muscle.
Patients often have the misconception that if they do not repair the biceps, they will not be
able to flex their elbow.
Distal biceps tendinopathy (often read as torn on MRI and often referred to as a partial tear)
should be easily distinguished from acute complete distal biceps tendon rupture based on
swelling and ecchymosis and loss of supination strength rather than pain-inhibited strength.

The hook test is sensitive and specific for complete distal biceps tendon rupture. This
maneuver is performed by having the patient flex the elbow to 90° and supinate the
arm. The examiner’s index finger hooks the undersurface or lateral surface of the distal
biceps tendon from the lateral side of the elbow (Figure 2). With an intact or partially
intact distal biceps tendon, the examiner’s finger can be inserted only approximately 1
cm. The unwary examiner may mistakenly hook the lacertus fibrosus. O’Driscoll et al10
reported that the hook test is associated with a sensitivity and specificity of 100% with
regard to identification of distal biceps tendon rupture.
Clinicians should anticipate this misconception and explain the role of the brachialis.
Flexion weakness, if present, usually is temporary and the result of pain.
In patients with an acute rupture, MRIs may show the tendon still reaching almost all the
way to the tuberosity, often with a few nonfunctional strands of tissue reaching the
tuberosity. Supination strength is diminished, and the tendon often is pulled off the
tuberosity during surgical management with a modest amount of force.

Imaging Studies
The diagnosis of distal biceps tendon rupture is made based on patient history and physical
examination findings.
Radiography, MRI, or ultrasonography may be helpful to plan surgical management,
particularly delayed surgical management in which retraction may inspire readiness for a
tendon graft.

Imaging Studies
In patients presenting for initial evaluation of anterior elbow pain and full elbow motion,
radiographs are of low diagnostic utility and unnecessary. In patients with a distal biceps
tendon rupture, radiographs may identify a fleck of bone from the insertion.
Ultrasonography or MRI may be helpful if the diagnosis is uncertain or for planning
delayed surgical management if concern exists with regard to the amount of retraction
of the tendon (Figure 3). The flexed-abducted-supinated position for MRI is used to
visualize most of the biceps tendon because it positions the tendon in a continuous
plane. The flexed-abducted-supinated view helps delineate the degree of tendinosis in
an intact tendon.
Ultrasonography may be helpful as an office-based and less expensive alternative to MRI
but depends on operator and equipment factors.

Management
Decision making
Patients must consider the discomfort, inconvenience (eg, time not permitted to use the arm
for strength), and potential harm they are willing to trade for modestly stronger supination.
Clinicians can be attentive to common misconceptions and ensure that patients select
treatment based on factors that matter most to them rather than based on misconceptions.
Nonsurgical Management

Nonsurgical management is an option for tendinopathy diagnosed as partial tear and rupture
of the small head alone, particularly in patients who can accommodate transient discomfort or
slight loss of supination strength
Nonsurgical management of complete distal biceps tendon ruptures is an option. Factors to
consider include the following:
Dominant or nondominant arm
Limited use of strong supination
Notable medical comorbidities (infirmity)
Patients treated nonsurgically experience modestly less mean supination strength compared
with those who undergo surgical repair.
Patients who elect to not undergo surgical treatment to reattach the distal biceps tendon
achieve a mean supination strength 60% of the contralateral side compared with 80% to 90%
supination strength after surgical treatment.
Some patients may experience a slight decrease in flexion strength (mean strength is >90%).
The degree to which patients experience loss of supination endurance and associated pain
with surgical or nonsurgical treatment is an area of uncertainty and debate.

Nonsurgical Management
With nonsurgical management of complete distal biceps tendon ruptures, patients are
permitted to immediately resume activities without restrictions. Conversely, surgical
management may lead to a period of immobilization or restricted use followed by
limited activity until the tendon heals.
In a study of patients with distal biceps ruptures that were not reattached, Morrey et al11
reported 30% less elbow flexion strength and 40% less supination strength compared
with the uninjured side. Endurance with supination decreased by 79% and endurance
with flexion decreased by 30%.11 In another study comparing nonsurgical and surgical
management, Freeman et al12 reported median supination strength of 74% and 92%,
respectively, and median elbow flexion strength of 93% and 95%, respectively. The mean
Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire score was 14 (population
norm, 6), indicating little discomfort or incapability.

Without an intact biceps, supination is driven by the brachioradialis and supinator
muscles. The brachioradialis is a strong supinator from pronation to neutral forearm
rotation; however, it functions more as a pronator from neutral to terminal supination.13
Similarly, the moment arm of the supinator declines between neutral and terminal
supination.13 Therefore, patients must adapt when performing activities requiring strong
supination with their arm by their side. The supination weakness may be more apparent
with tasks performed away from the body, such as changing a lightbulb.13 Regardless,
many patients who decide not to undergo the distal biceps reattachment accommodate
well.
Surgical Management
Indications
Patients with a complete distal biceps tendon rupture may elect to undergo surgical treatment
to reattach the tendon if they value supination strength and are concerned about an unknown
potential for fatigue pain.
Whether the scars and contours after repair are more aesthetic than nonsurgical management
remains unclear.
Patients with an isolated tear of the short head of the distal biceps tendon that is causing
symptoms 1 year postinjury may be offered reattachment.
Contraindications
Infirmity
Severe elbow or forearm stiffness from previous injury or disease
Inability to commit to at least 4 months of activity limitations postoperatively
>Problems with the skin of the antecubital fossa

Numerous exposures and fixation methods

Surgical Management
Palpation or MRI, if available, can help identify the location of the torn biceps tendon.
Alternatively, if not visible or palpable at the time of surgical management, a second,
more proximal incision can be made to locate the tendon stump; however, this would be
unusual.
The patient is placed in the supine position with the arm on a hand table to allow access
to the proximal forearm and the antecubital fossa. A sterile tourniquet affords access to
a biceps that is retracted more than expected. A nonsterile tourniquet may be adequate
in most patients.
In the past, the single-incision anterior approach involved the use of an extensile, volar
Henry approach. A smaller anterior approach usually is sufficient. The approach starts
just distal to the antecubital fossa, with an incision along the proximal portion of the
volar Henry approach to the forearm. The basilic vein and the lateral antebrachial
cutaneous nerve (LABCN) are identified laterally and protected to avoid excessive
retraction on the LABCN.

Via a small incision, the surgeon will not be able to determine a muscle interval. After the
fascia is incised, edema and blood are released. The surgeon can then stick a finger up
proximally in the plane in which the blood was present, locate the tendon with the
finger, and pull the tendon down with the finger or a clamp. Occasionally, if the tendon
stump cannot be felt or pulled down easily or safely, a more proximal incision is made to
feed the stump into the antecubital incision.
Distally, the track in which the biceps tendon used to run usually can be identified easily
and confirmed by placing a finger in the tract and palpating the biceps tuberosity with
little or no effort. This area can then be opened adequately for safe placement of
anchors or a button, usually with limited blunt spreading and little additional dissection.
After a delay of more than a few weeks, location of the track of the biceps down to the
radius may not be easy. If this occurs, the surgeon can make a larger skin incision and
identify and open the interval between the brachioradialis and the pronator teres. If the
track of the biceps is not clear, visualization—rather than palpation—of the biceps
tuberosity is best. For a larger exposure, surgeons should identify, ligate, and divide the
vessels that cross the interval distal to the usual course of the biceps (the so-called leash
of Henry, the recurrent branches of the radial artery). The LABCN can be identified as it
exits between the biceps and brachialis in the antecubital fossa. The posterior
interosseous nerve does not need to be identified via this approach because it is
protected by keeping the forearm in maximal supination and limiting excessive lateral
retraction. After the radial tuberosity is identified, a bare area will be observed at the
medial edge of the tuberosity at which the distal biceps tendon was inserted. Sizable
remnants of the distal biceps tendon may be débrided off the tuberosity. Originally,
surgeons believed insertion of the tendon into a trough in the radial tuberosity was
necessary to attain healing; however, surgeons currently understand that a tendon
suture against the bone will heal without a trough and without scraping or drilling the
surface of the bone to encourage bleeding. Maintenance of tuberosity height allows for
improved supination strength by preserving the supination cam of the tuberosity.6

Multiple techniques are available to secure the distal biceps tendon to the radius. Via a
single-incision anterior approach if the tendon is not inset into the bone, options include
a suture button or suture anchors. If the tendon is inset into the bone, options include a
button, an interference screw, or sutures passed through bone tunnels. Surgeons should
attempt to secure the tendon on the medial side of the radial tuberosity to restore the
cam effect. One option is to place drill holes from lateral to medial through the base of
the radial tuberosity, pass the two sutures through the holes from lateral to medial, and
tie the sutures together on the medial side after cinching the tendon down to bone.
Suture anchor fixation typically is achieved with one anchor distally and the other
proximally along the ulnar margin of the footprint. One limb of the suture is passed up
and back via a running locking stitch. The second limb is passed through the tendon
proximal to a locking stitch to function as a sliding stitch. The short head of the tendon is

radial tuberosity to guide the reamer through the anterior cortex only, which allows the
tendon to be inset into this wide hole. A bioabsorbable tenodesis screw is then used to
secure the biceps tendon in this hole. The screw should be positioned as radial as
possible to seat the tendon as ulnar as possible. The ends of the suture are then tied
over the top of the screw as a secondary means of fixation. Concerns have been raised
regarding reaction or foreign-body effects from absorbable screws, or fractures
associated with increased hoop stresses from interference screws.
Suspensory cortical button fixation is achieved by making a trough hole and then
penetrating the dorsal cortex with the use of a Beath pin or a drill. The button is then
secured to the tendon at a length that will allow flipping and result in insetting of the
tendon. Sutures are used to pass the button through the hole in the dorsal cortex and
flip it so it engages the dorsal cortex, securing the tendon (Video 1).

The most common complication after distal biceps tendon repair is dysfunction of the

Direct repair to olecranon via bone tunnels

Primary Repair
A posterior, longitudinal, midline incision is made from the junction of the middle and
distal third of the brachium to the midportion of the olecranon. Full-thickness flaps are
raised off triceps tendon. The ulnar nerve is identified and protected.28,31,36
An associated avulsed bony fragment, if present, can be fixed with the use of a screw
and washer or tension band construct. More frequently, the fragment is excised, and the
tendon is reattached to bone.26
The ruptured tendon ends are débrided and mobilized. With mobilization up to the
musculotendinous junction, ruptures as much as several weeks old can be successfully
repaired.34 The insertion point on the olecranon is prepared with the use of a
combination of a rongeur and curettes.36
For direct repair via bone tunnels, heavy, nonabsorbable sutures are passed through the
tendon via a Krackow or Bunnell suture configuration, attached to the olecranon via
crossed transosseous 2.5-mm tunnels, and tied over the bone bridge.26,27,33 A Krackow
suture pattern is accomplished by passing a suture retrograde through the center of the
distal tendon and performing a running locking pattern up one side of the tendon and
then down the other side to exit out the center of the distal tendon. A Bunnell
configuration also begins retrograde at the distal tendon and weaves up the tendon in a
lazy S-pattern and then back down the other side in an opposing S-pattern to form an
intratendinous series of X’s.
Several bone bridge techniques have been described.
Two crossing tunnels in an X pattern drilled 1 cm from the olecranon tip to the dorsal
olecranon30 (Figure 10)

For direct repair with the use of suture anchors, single- and double-row constructs are
available.
Single-row suture anchor repair is performed with the use of two to three anchors (4.5 to
5.0 mm) at the center of the footprint. The Krackow sutures are then tied to the sutures
from the anchors.27,36 Do not débride past cortical bone if using anchors because it will
compromise pull-out strength.
A double-row construct (also called transosseous equivalent) has been described by Yeh
et al.37 Suture anchors are placed at the proximal footprint and then secured to knotless
anchors at the distal footprint.27
In biomechanical studies, the double-row construct has been reported to result in less
displacement and an anatomic footprint compared with transosseous tunnels or single-
row anchors; however, no difference in ultimate peak load and yield strength were
noted.26-28
Acute repair is accomplished under minimal tension with the elbow positioned in 30°
to 45° of flexion.
Repair with autograft or allograft augmentation for poor tissue quality
If the distal tendon has poor tissue quality, the following options are available:
After excising the degenerative distal tendon back to healthy tendon, a V-Y turndown
can be performed to achieve primary repair to the insertion if the defect is small.30
Allograft or autograft augmentation can be performed. Plantaris, palmaris longus, or
flexor carpi radialis autograft or Achilles tendon allograft can be woven through the
triceps tendon or can be overlayed for augmentation. The native triceps tendon
should be secured to the insertion before placing the graft.30,31
An olecranon-based forearm fascial flap also can be rotated to augment repair31
(Figure 11).

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Differentiating tendon from scarring may be difficult in patients with a subacute/chronic
rupture; dissection may need to be extended proximally to locate native tissue.
Do not débride past cortical bone if an anchor is being used, and always predrill anchors so
they do not break in cortical bone. A single anchor is insufficient; always use at least two
suture anchors.30,33
Always identify and protect the ulnar nerve
Plan strategies to make suture knots less prominent
Avoid push-ups and deep elbow flexion exercises for 6 months postoperatively30

Outcomes
In general, patients who undergo acute primary triceps repair achieve acceptable strength and
range of motion by 1 year postoperatively.

Outcomes
The reported outcomes of surgical fixation of triceps ruptures consist mostly of small
case series. If repaired within 3 weeks, usually acceptable strength and range of motion
are present. van Riet et al29 reported that all patients who underwent acute repair
achieved 4 out of 5 triceps strength but had a mean loss of 10° of terminal extension,
with an mean of 136° of elbow motion. In another series, eight of nine patients had full
motion at 6 week postoperatively, and heterotopic ossification at the distal triceps
occurred in one patient. This patient underwent heterotopic ossification excision to
regain motion.27 Most patients who undergo acute primary repair regain near full
strength but may lose 5° to 10° of full extension.28 At 1 year postoperatively, patients
reach peak strength of 80% and endurance strength of 99%.33
Patients generally are satisfied with distal triceps repair. In a case series, 9 of 11 patients
were satisfied and had full return to activity.26 In a larger series, 95% of 55 patients were
satisfied and stated they would undergo surgical treatment again.38 In addition, of 37
military patients, 86% were satisfied and were able to perform a mean of 54 push-ups.
Of these service personnel, 97% remained on active duty.32
Outcomes are slightly inferior in patients who undergo chronic repair or reconstruction
despite regaining functional ability.26 These patients have lower peak strength and
slower return to activity compared with patients who undergo primary, acute repair.27,36

Although historically, transosseous bone tunnels are the more common surgical repair
option, considerable differences have not been reported compared with suture anchor
repair. In a cohort of 55 patients who underwent transosseous or suture anchor repair,
no substantial difference in pain scores or the re-rupture rate was noted.38 A
biomechanical study on six-stranded, double-row suture anchor repair versus six-
stranded transosseous repair reported equivalent displacement under tension.39
Tran et al40 explored the outcomes of reattachment of distal triceps ruptures. Of the 593
surgically managed elbows, preinjury level of function was achieved in 92%. All the
elbows recovered grade 4 or grade 5 strength. The 15% complication rate included a 5%
retear rate.
Alkhafan et al41 reviewed 25 studies that included 2,586 distal biceps repair procedures.
The authors reported that the suture anchor repair technique resulted in lower revision
surgery; higher postoperative Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand scores; less
time undergoing medical care; and lower rates of infection compared with transosseous
repair.
